entries.title: Deportations Are Spiking. Judges Say Their Hands Are Being Forced.
entries.summary: Trump administration’s mass firings of immigration judges are influencing court outcomes, they say.
entries.content:
The Trump administration has created a climate of fear among the nation's immigration judges, firing those who don't go along with sweeping policy changes meant to boost deportations.

The Justice Department, which manages the nation's immigration court system, is relying on pressure campaigns to bend outcomes to match President Donald Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement vision, one current and three recently terminated judges told NOTUS.

They also said the department leadership has adopted new strategies to limit their discretion to rule in immigrants’ favor, which has effectively led to more deportations.

One current judge, who spoke on condition of anonymity over fear of reprisal, said colleagues were deciding cases with a new understanding that “following the law can risk their job if that law is inconsistent with current policy.”

“There's also a lot of fear among the immigration judges. The fact that following the law in a court is bravery is a little concerning,” the current judge said, before correcting themself. “That's a lot concerning.”

The Executive Office of Immigration Review, the Justice agency that houses the courts, has fired around 125 immigration judges since Trump took office. Nearly all of them received only an email with a couple sentences explaining that the president was asserting his authority under the Constitution.

The firings have continued in recent weeks. Additionally, around 100 additional judges have left with separation incentives or to retire, meaning more than one-in-four has left government.

While staff stressed they seek to implement the law in a neutral manner, the firings have effectively pushed judges to grant relief less often.

“For most of my colleagues, they’re going to do what they need to do to keep their job,” said Brea Burgie, a Colorado-based immigration judge who was fired in June.

“There is the constant stress of, ‘Is this the thing I'm going to do that gets me fired?’ When you’re living with that, the path of least resistance is, you don’t want to lose your job so you just comply,” Burgie said.

Some judges, who are also voluntarily leaving at unprecedented rates, have decided they cannot stay on the job in good conscience because they can't apply the law fairly.

“They're leaving because they feel like they can no longer execute due process,” the current judge said. “If you're a judge and you can't uphold due process in your court, or you feel like you can't effectuate that because policies are being made around you that don't allow you to to provide due process to people, that's a big concern for you because you feel like you are actually breaking the law.”

The second Trump administration has overhauled the deportation system to limit judges' latitude, former and current judges said, through new legal interpretations and policy memos that dictate how judges should run their courtrooms.

There are new requirements for faster decisions. The current judge noted they have little control over their schedule and anyone above them could be calling the shots on the movement of cases.

EOIR has packed as many as 150 cases for administrative actions on a judge’s docket some mornings, often with asylum seekers receiving little notice. If the migrants do not show up for the proceeding, judges must issue removal orders in absentia.

All of those factors appear to be bearing fruit for the Trump administration. After remaining relatively stable for much of Trump’s current term, according to the Transaction Records Access Clearinghouse, immigrant removal orders climbed this spring and spiked by 30% in June.

In some cases, threats to judges have been explicit.

In January, after a back-and-forth between Justice and federal courts over the legality of banning certain immigrants from being released from detention while awaiting court proceedings, Burgie received an email threatening discipline if she continued allowing bond hearings.

Burgie continued to do so, leaning on the federal court’s precedent. Days later, she was removed from cases involving detained immigrants. Months after that, she was fired. Like others, she was given no notice and had to leave immediately.

Eva Saltzman, a Chicago-based immigration judge, was in the middle of a hearing on July 30 when she received an email saying she was fired “effective immediately.”

“I read it again to make sure I understood it correctly,” Saltzman said. “I advised the parties we would be concluding immediately that we would not be able to complete that hearing that day.”

Saltzman then packed up her office and headed home.

She was the most senior judge on the bench in Chicago. She never let her guard down in the second Trump administration because she knew her location in a Democratic city and her low rate of deportation orders would put her on the Trump administration’s radar.

“As the agenda and the goals of the administration evolved and became more clear, I was concerned that doing my job in the way that I had always done would lead to me being terminated,” Saltzman said. “And I think that’s in part what happened here.”

Emmett Soper, a Virginia-based immigration judge who was fired last September, called that fear a “pretty effective technique” to achieve more deportations. Judges often have latitude in their decision making, he said, noting the same set of facts in many cases could allow a grant or denial to an immigrant’s request.

“If you have one of these cases where you are deciding whether to grant or deny, if you have this very real threat hanging over your head, it’s only human to be cognizant of that,” Soper said. “The judges are only human beings. They need to support themselves and their families.”

The Justice Department's moves have helped reduce the backlog of pending cases from its peak of 4 million to around 3.2 million.

A Justice spokesperson, when asked whether EOIR is targeting certain judges or seeking to influence court outcomes through personnel policy, said the department was looking to correct errors committed by its predecessors.

“After four years of the Biden administration forcing immigration courts to implement a de facto amnesty for hundreds of thousands of aliens, this Department of Justice is restoring integrity to our immigration system and encourages talented legal professionals to join in our mission to protect national security and public safety,” the spokesperson said.

The Justice Department is hiring new immigration judges to keep up with the departures. The department is advertising open positions as “deportation judges” and has eliminated some requirements for relevant experience

EOIR has onboarded 190 judges in fiscal year 2026, easily surpassing its previous hiring record for a fiscal year, including 118 since May. Nearly 90% of that more recent group were attorneys for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the military or prosecutorial offices. The department typically hired a large swath of its judges from immigration-focused private firms, but it has recently selected just a handful who had non-ICE immigration experience.

The current immigration judge noted the new hires are also receiving less training than they used to, which could mean cases that have been cleared might come back down after appeals because of rookie mistakes.

“They're all learning the immigration law and learning how to run their courts all at the same time,” the current judge said.
entries.author: Eric Katz

entries.title: Garbage Contaminating Camps In Gaza Renews Calls For U.S. Pressure On Israel
entries.summary: Lawmakers and the United Nations are warning of the spread of disease because of the unsanitary conditions in which most Palestinians are living.
entries.content:
The United Nations recently reported that most Palestinians in Gaza are living steps away from open sewage or human waste, and the strip is overflowing with garbage and rubble. Disease is spreading rapidly, and humanitarian groups and some lawmakers are redoubling demands for the U.S. to pressure Israel to ease overcrowding and stop blocking aid.

Dire conditions for those living in Gaza have persisted despite the 2025 agreement brokered by the Trump administration between Israel and the Palestinian militant group Hamas. An assessment cited by the U.N. in early April found that 60 percent of Gaza’s population was exposed to sewage or human waste within about 10 yards of their shelters, while more than 900,000 Palestinians were exposed to accumulated garbage in residential areas.

Data gathered July 19-25 by the World Health Organization suggested the two top health problems among Palestinians — acute respiratory infections and acute diarrhea — stemmed from poor conditions of water, sanitation and hygiene, also known by the acronym WASH. The U.N. also reported “significant” numbers of skin disease cases driven by clean water shortages. A U.N. WASH report earlier in July said 86 percent of households struggle to access a toilet or latrine, while 17 percent have observed open defecation. And the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem reported this summer “an extreme outbreak of rats and pests” in camps packed with displaced families, noting the link to garbage overflow, cesspits and rodent-borne disease.

“Sanitation is a chain, and all the chain has been devastated,” said Roba Daour Ziara, a Gaza-based public health officer at the charity Oxfam. She noted waste should normally move from toilets to treatment facilities, but Israeli attacks have destroyed hundreds of those facilities. The ones that remain need maintenance and power, rendered out of reach because Israeli authorities have sharply limited deliveries of repair materials, fuel, lubricant oil and generators, according to Oxfam and the U.N.

Earlier this month, 65 House Democrats — led by Reps. Andrea Salinas of Oregon and Kweisi Mfume of Maryland — wrote to President Donald Trump warning of “rodent and pest infestations throughout displacement camps … and insufficient rebuilding of the infrastructure needed for sewage, water and electricity.” The lawmakers blasted Israel’s restrictions on goods that it says have both civilian and military uses, as well as its limits on the normal operations of international aid groups. Tel Aviv’s approach “undermines a key component of the 20-point plan,” they wrote, referring to Trump’s stated roadmap for peace.

Even as Palestinians struggle, the Trump administration has said it will deliver stability and Israeli-Palestinian harmony through the president’s Board of Peace, most recently by announcing a plan for Hamas to disarm. Skeptics of the approach argue that the living conditions of Palestinians must be addressed to achieve meaningful progress toward regional peace.

“The President has a bold and ambitious plan to rebuild Gaza, which is well underway due to the efforts of the Board of Peace,” a State Department spokesperson told NOTUS via email. “US advocacy has enabled gains across key sectors: food assistance now reaches a majority of the population, health and nutrition services have expanded, and WASH support has scaled up, resulting in measurable improvements in food security, health outcomes, and access to safe water, along with temporary shelter support.”

Israel’s embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment. Israeli officials have said they are facilitating appropriate deliveries.

“Israel remains committed to the coordination of humanitarian aid to ensure the appropriate medical, nutritional, and WASH response remains available to the Gazan civilian population,” Israel’s Coordination of Government Activities in the Territories unit said in a statement on X last week. The post listed Israeli approvals of shipments of generator spare parts by the U.N. and water containers by the Red Cross.

But Ziara noted that Oxfam and other aid organizations say Palestinians in Gaza still effectively face a “blockade,” and that improvements in humanitarian conditions are fragile and irregular.

Humanitarian groups, Ziara said, are seeking consistent engine oil flow to support daily services, not just specific operations; advocacy to shield WASH infrastructure from Israeli airstrikes; and more generators since Gaza remains without electricity — which means water treatment facilities share generators, limiting their output. She also noted that the growing section of Gaza controlled by Israeli forces includes many landfills. Without the ability to reach those sites, groups that collect solid waste, including the U.N. and Palestinian municipal workers, are instead using temporary dumping stations that are often located between Palestinian encampments.

Rachel Norris, the Gaza response director at the nonprofit Mercy Corps, said Gaza residents’ makeshift solutions fall short.

“Instead of large waste management trucks or any of the sort of facilities that would normally run, you are seeing donkeys pulling carts filled with waste,” she said, while some Palestinians have also built trenches or other temporary sites to contain waste. The result is latrines that Norris compared to “using a porta-potty that is not being changed out.”

A July 23 U.N. report found that 69% of the 181 displacement centers it assessed had visible sewage. At some sites, families were resorting to using slipshod toilets, buckets or plastic bags.

Meanwhile, amid shortages of clean water, Norris said, families face “impossible choices” about whether to use it for drinking, cooking, bathing or cleaning.

Addressing WASH is “foundational” and arguably even more important than increases in food supplies, according to Stacy Gilbert, a former State Department official who worked on global crises for over 20 years.

“You can keep feeding food into the situation, but if you’ve got poor sanitation it literally comes out the other end,” she said.

Gilbert resigned from her State Department role in 2024, citing the U.S. backing of Israel’s Gaza offensive. She described how some of the most vulnerable groups face outsize risks: When mothers are malnourished, they often supplement breast milk with formula, but even if that is available, it is dangerous to make with contaminated water.

Amid continued Israeli strikes and a deepening humanitarian crisis, Gilbert said the most dangerous part for Palestinians could be the lack of global attention to what’s happening on the ground, with garbage or debris left to rot and unexploded bombs littering the landscape.

“In many ways,” she said, “it's a more dangerous situation now because the world thinks the war is over.”

entries.title: No Comment
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 18, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

D.C. public safety leaders — including U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro and interim D.C. Police Chief Jeffery Carroll — were slated to discuss violent crime trends at a rare joint public meeting last night. But the event was canceled, with little explanation as to why.

The public event was sure to be a minefield at a time when a crime statistics scandal is roiling the D.C. police department, an ongoing surge in federal law enforcement and National Guard deployment has outraged city activists, and Pirro’s recent spat with President Donald Trump has made headlines and raised questions about whether she’ll keep her job.

Free D.C., a group of local anti-Trump activists who have loudly opposed Pirro, had been encouraging D.C. residents to show up to the meeting and make their voices heard.

Now, “it seems pretty clear that they don't actually want to hear from D.C. residents,” said Free D.C. co-founder Alex Dodds, speaking about Pirro and the Trump administration.

It’s not the first time something like this has happened: The event had previously been scheduled for June, but it was postponed. This time, the organizer — D.C.’s Criminal Justice Coordinating Council — made no promises that it would be rescheduled. Asked to explain the reason for the cancellation, CJCC spokesperson Margarita Mikhaylova said they “do not have additional information to share.”

“Our focus now is on determining the best approach for future public engagement,” she wrote in an email. A Pirro spokesperson referred questions about the event to the CJCC.





DEEP DIVE

Five summers ago, the Nationals acquired an outfielder named Donovan Casey as part of a blockbuster trade. The next spring, in April 2022, the Nats called up Casey from the minors, inching him right to the edge of his lifelong dream.

But, as NOTUS' Jesse Dougherty writes in a longform profile, this is where Casey's baseball journey gets complicated. For five days, he sat on the bench for the Nationals, preparing — both mentally and physically — for an opportunity that never came. While he packed up to head back to the minors, Sean Doolittle, then the team's closer, told Casey he would be back.

Casey agreed, still confident even at a low point that he would return to the major leagues. But he never did.

The following years were tough, including panic attacks and long stretches of doubt. Casey left long voice memos for his wife, saying through tears that he wasn't strong enough, wasn't fast enough, wasn't a good enough hitter. Eventually, though, he learned to live with getting so close to his ultimate goal without reaching it. The question now, years later: Does he consider himself a big leaguer, even though he never played a game?

L1024044.jpg (8019x5351, AR: 1.50)




FROM THE DISTRICT

A woman was killed by a driver in Northeast D.C. over the weekend, Fox 5 reports. It’s the 28th traffic fatality of the year.

That number is a notable increase from last year, which saw 25 deaths through the entire year. But rather than being a spike, it’s more of a troubling return to the city’s usual numbers. On average, there were 36.2 traffic fatalities annually over the past 10 years. In both 2023 and 2024, 52 people died in traffic accidents. Still, as The Washington Post reported, a return to those numbers runs counter to the promises of soon-to-be-former Mayor Muriel Bowser, who vowed in 2015 to get traffic fatalities to zero.

The District might soon control the D.C. Armory — the longtime home of the D.C. National Guard — rather than the National Park Service, the Washington Business Journal reports.

More than 220 manhole covers had to be welded shut ahead of the Freedom 250 Grand Prix this weekend. Why? City Cast DC asked a physicist.

A Catholic-run boarding house in Northeast D.C., where young women could find below-market rents and community, has closed, NPR reports.





SPORTS

College football season is around the corner, but local fans may not have a whole lot to look forward to on Saturdays this fall. The Associated Press released its preseason Top 25 on Monday afternoon and Maryland is … nowhere to be found. Coming off a 4-8 season, the Terps are projected by ESPN to once again finish in the bottom half of the Big Ten.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Rangers, 8:05 p.m. (MLB.TV)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo by Kannetha Brown-Ngeth for NOTUS. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was A) RFK Stadium. In 2002, there was an American Le Mans series race in the stadium’s parking lots. A special shout-out to Halle Czechowski, who answered first.

entries.title: Republicans vs. the Polls
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Why one smart Republican is still looking forward to November. Florida, Florida, Florida. The downstream impact of bad polls. A Cornyn staffer joined Team Talarico. And: Gaza’s garbage crisis.  





THE LATEST

Republicans do not believe the hype: Recent weeks have seen the whirring and chirping to life of the various election prognostication machines we’ll all be refreshing between now and November. They differ when it comes to the Senate — control there is either a toss-up or a slight Democratic advantage, depending on which you like best. But for the House, they all say the same thing: Republicans will not be in control when all the counting is over.

Behind that consensus: Donald Trump’s flatlining poll numbers, huge turnout for Democrats in primaries and special elections, generic ballot averages showing Democrats with a lead. Add the historic headwinds for the party not in the White House in a midterm.

“A midterm after you win the presidential is tough, but I think that [pundits] are ignoring some of the fundamentals of this cycle,” a senior Republican strategist told NOTUS’ Jasmine Wright yesterday.

Those fundamentals: Redistricting, money and the Supreme Court. “You’re not gonna see a 30-, 40-, 50-seat swing because of redistricting, frankly,” the strategist said. Republicans need to win “basically 12” of 18 truly toss-up seats to keep their majority, they went on. The massive Republican war chest has been well covered, but less so the impact of the court’s June ruling on party–candidate spending coordination.

This is nerdy but potentially powerful stuff. The Republican Party machine has money the Democratic machine does not have. When billionaires drop their independent expenditure ads, it’s helpful, but those folks tend to do their own thing, message-wise.

“We may be being outspent by Democrats in specific House races, but because all their money’s in outside groups, we’re actually getting more weight behind our messages with less dollars,” the Republican strategist said.

The wildcard: Voters who still haven’t tuned in. “There’s an information gap with voters,” the Republican strategist said. “I think once we are able to tell our story with that money working more efficiently, and making a good contrast between us and Democrats, these races are going to be super close.”

For the expected Democratic eyeroll at all this, look to tonight’s primaries in Florida. The state has been redistricted in a Republican image. Money is flying around. And it’s not hard to get the GOP message out in a state so wholly controlled by the party. And yet: “They thought they were going to easily pick up seats in Florida by gerrymandering, and that’s not the case,” Madison Andrus, who covers Florida at the DCCC, told NOTUS’ Manuela Silva. “They are still having to spend and compete in districts they thought they had locked up because their agenda has failed so spectacularly.”

Open tabs: 60 days after signing Iran deal, Trump stuck in quagmire as war drags on (WaPo); Deportations Are Spiking. Judges Say Their Hands Are Being Forced. (NOTUS); Mary Peltola Shakes Up Senate Campaign Staff Days Before Alaska Primary (NYT)





From Florida


Democrats have their own problems: A couple of contentious House primaries tonight could make the party confidence mentioned above a little tempered. The extremely messy one in Florida’s 20th, one of the safest blue seats left in the state, has Black leaders seething at Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, who is trying to stay in Congress in a new seat that has long been seen as a Black seat by Democrats.

And in Florida’s 25th, Rep. Jared Moskowitz is facing down a DSA primary challenge from Oliver Larkin. “I think if Moskowitz were to lose this primary, I think Republicans might be favored in that district,” Kyle Kondik, one of the election prognosticators at the University of Virginia, told NOTUS’ Jasmine Wright on C-SPAN yesterday.

The Republicans have their own angst-inducing primary tonight. The party establishment is hoping that incendiary outsider candidate James Fishback does not have a great showing in the gubernatorial primary. Trump has endorsed Rep. Byron Donalds. Trump, by the way, voted by mail in that race.

From the campaign trail


Bad polls make for jam-packed primaries: Get ready for a boatload of candidates to enter the 2028 field on vibes alone, NOTUS’ Christa Dutton reports. High-profile polling misses in Democratic primaries this month (you know the ones) mean basically anyone can talk themselves into believing the numbers are meaningless and run regardless of what the data may say. “We are going to enter an election season where there are a bajillion new sources of information, and no standard way to figure out which one means what,” Ben Wikler, the former chair of the Wisconsin Democratic Party, told Christa.

Popular local eateries full of potential interview subjects, your time has returned! Wikler said Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary polls didn’t capture what he thinks is the most telling measure of a candidate’s chances: conversations with voters. Hope you like having a microphone repeatedly stuck in your face at your favorite coffee place, any given South Carolinian!

Scoop: James Talarico hires Cornyn staffer. A former top aide to Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) has gone to work for the Democrat trying to replace him, NOTUS’ Igor Bobic and Reese Gorman scooped yesterday. Cornyn deputy legislative director Jacob Smith has signed on to the Talarico campaign as deputy political director. Smith previously worked on the House Science Committee for Rep. Mike Collins (R-Georgia) and was a legislative aide for Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi).

First on NOTUS: The Pete Stauber bump? Alaskans picking a senator will soon be getting advice from a Minnesotan, with the help of six figures worth of ads. Sen. Dan Sullivan’s campaign for reelection is going up with a spot featuring Stauber, a Republican representing Minnesota’s 8th Congressional District. In the ad, Stauber attacks the bipartisan bona fides of former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. NOTUS’ Al Weaver got the first look at the ad, which starts running tomorrow after the primary where Sullivan and Peltola are expected to emerge for the general.





NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Sports desk: He Spent Five Days With the Nats But Never Played. Is He a Big Leaguer? By Jesse Dougherty





NEW ON NOTUS

Aid workers plead for help with Gaza’s garbage crisis: “Sanitation is a chain, and all the chain has been devastated,” Gaza-based Oxfam public health officer Roba Daour Ziara told NOTUS recently. Our Akbar Shahid Ahmed and Hamed Ahmadi report that growing evidence of dire sanitary conditions for refugees packed into displacement camps has created an acute public health emergency.

The two top health problems among Palestinians stem from poor conditions of water, sanitation and hygiene, according to World Health Organization data gathered in late July. Amid shortages of clean water, families face “impossible choices” about whether to use it for drinking, cooking, bathing or cleaning, one aid official said.

To correct this, public health officials want big changes to how aid flows into Gaza. The Israeli government says it is doing enough to address the issue. The U.S. State Department told NOTUS that the agreement brokered between Hamas and Israel last year has “scaled up” sanitation help.

Aid workers tell NOTUS they fear the dangerous aftermath of the worst days of the conflict between Israel and Hamas is fading from public view. They have some allies in Congress: Earlier this month, 65 House Democrats — led by Reps. Andrea Salinas of Oregon and Kweisi Mfume of Maryland — warned the White House that continued restrictions on aid to Gaza “undermines a key component” of Trump’s plan to rebuild the region.

More: Texas Families Ask the Supreme Court to Keep Ten Commandments Out of the Classroom, by Jenna Monnin

Fake Poll Showing LA Mayor Karen Bass Leading Was a ‘Social Experiment,’ Group Says, by Jackie Llanos

Planned Parenthood Plans Its Biggest Ad Buy of 2026 Against Susan Collins, by Torrie Herrington





NOT US

  • Islamophobia’s Rise in Texas: ‘I Won’t Rest Until Every Muslim Is Gone,’ by J. David Goodman, Lauren McGaughy, Jesus Jiménez and Ruth Graham for The New York Times
  • Trump weighs a plan for press briefings when Leavitt leaves, sources say, by Kristen Holmes, Adam Cancryn and Alayna Treene for CNN
  • We Tracked a Shipment of Rare Books. It Ended at an Amazon AI Training Facility, by Emanuel Maiberg for 404 Media




Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS Newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If this newsletter was shared with you, please sign up — it’s free! Have a tip? Email us at tips@notus.com. And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@notus.com.

entries.title: He Spent Five Days With the Nats But Never Played. Is He a Big Leaguer?
entries.summary: Donovan Casey made it to the cusp of his lifelong dream. His biggest challenge has been learning to live with that.
entries.content:
Rutland, Vermont, is an hour forty-five from Burlington, almost four to Boston and very, very far from Major League Baseball. And so there are times — random times, like in the time it takes to drive from home to work in the predawn darkness — that Donovan Casey starts thinking again.

What if, he wonders to himself, the manager had had me pinch run? 

What if he had put me in as a defensive sub?

What if I had gotten one at-bat and hit a fucking homer?

But wait … hold on a second … what if I had gotten one at-bat and struck out on three pitches? 

It’s not productive, necessarily. Just human. For five days in April 2022, Casey was on the Washington Nationals, checking off almost every verb expected of a new major leaguer. The outfielder called his wife and parents. He hustled to Pittsburgh. He looked at the uniform in his locker, his name on the back, the No. 44 right under it. Then he jogged, threw and stretched. He put the uniform on, a warmup jacket over it, then took the jacket off to stretch some more in the dugout. He then traveled with the team to D.C. He received another jersey in another locker. He did not, however, play at any point. And that’s why what if is burrowed in his brain.

***

THERE IS A PUBLIC SPREADSHEET on the internet titled “Near Major Leaguers.” Compiled by a man named Bill Hickman for the Society for American Baseball Research, it does exactly what it promises, cataloging the players who came so close to their childhood dream but never made it onto the field.

Donovan Casey occupies cell No. 92, sandwiched between William Clifford “Bill” “Cliff” Case (1914, Brooklyn Tip-Tops, Federal League) and Joe Chabek (1915, Brooklyn Dodgers, National League). And on the far right side of the sheet, Hinman has tidbits for a handful of players, like …

Died while in military service during World War I.

Had won a contest that enabled him to travel with Sox as a player.

Middleweight boxing champ of the U.S. Navy. 

Was shot and killed on June 15, 1911 by a jealous husband.

Died in famous Duluth Dukes bus crash in 1948. He was the team’s manager & bus driver.

For Casey, though, there are no additional notes, so here goes: Born and raised in Stratford, New Jersey, he played at Boston College before the Dodgers drafted him in the 20th round in 2017. Ever since pro scouts came around, his only goal was to make enough to pay off his student loans, which he did with his signing bonus. After that, Casey figured, everything else would be extra. He had nothing to lose.
L1023885 copy.jpg (10594x7803, AR: 1.36)
Still, once he started climbing the Dodgers’ system, he wanted the majors more than anything. Then, in July 2021 — five years ago this summer — Casey was one of four players acquired by the Nationals in the Max Scherzer-Trea Turner trade. If there were obituaries for every baseball career, this would be in the first few lines of his, if not right there at the top. But the sport also took him to Cape Cod and Ogden, Utah. Rancho Cucamonga, California, and Tulsa, Oklahoma. Surprise, Arizona, to play in the Arizona Fall League; Harrisburg, Rochester and Wilmington to play for the Nats’ minor league teams; and then York, Pennsylvania, and Monterrey to play just a bit longer at the end.

And, yes, it took him to Pittsburgh and D.C. for those five days in 2022. They are not part of Major League Baseball’s official record, at least in the sense that he has no official stats. But that they happened can be confirmed by a simple fact: Donovan Casey was there.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“You had a dream as a kid to get to the big leagues and you got to the big leagues,” Casey, 30, married and a father of two, said this summer. “My wife says it all the time: ‘You did it. You got called up. Who the hell cares?’ And I don’t know, the way I look at it is …”

He hit pause for a few seconds. A stream of consciousness slowed down to a trickle.

“... you can play the what-ifs all you want …”

“ … but …”

“… you know … “

“ … so much of this shit is out of your control.” Another pause. “And there were so many times I wanted to quit.”Another pause. “But instead I kept going, like, what’s one more day?”
***
CASEY HAS NEVER BEEN able to sit still. When he was a kid, he threw a ball against the house so much that there’s no more mortar between the bricks. When a handful of teams were interested in drafting him as a pitcher, he couldn’t imagine sitting for days between each appearance, waiting with nothing else to do. And when the Nationals traded for him in 2022, Casey wanted to drive straight from Tulsa to Harrisburg, which was a solid plan except for that his wife wouldn’t have it. They spent one night in a hotel to split up the 18-hour trip.

“He’s just like that,” his wife, Mary, said. “He was so antsy to get there and get going.”

Which was also why, during those five days with the Nationals, Casey’s family kept reacting to false alarms. While everyone else in the stands watched the games, they were watching him, looking for any sign he might be going in. When he unzipped his warmup jacket in Pittsburgh, his friends, a rowdy crew from high school, perked up. When he stretched his legs in the late innings, his wife hoped it meant he was about to pinch-run.
IMG_9123 (3) copy.jpg (8640x5760, AR: 1.50)But on Friday, Saturday and Sunday at PNC Park, he remained on the bench. On Monday in D.C., it rained and a series opener with the Diamondbacks was postponed. There would be a doubleheader Tuesday. That, Casey figured, was when he would make his debut. It had to be, right? They would play 18 innings in one day, which meant there weren’t just two games he could start, but double the number of chances to pinch-hit, pinch-run or sub in on defense.

Then the first game came and went. Then, before the second game, Manager Dave Martinez put out the lineup and Casey’s name wasn’t on it. He went straight to the weight room and started lifting. Heavy, too, with extra reps in every set.

“I was in there thinking: What am I even doing here?” Casey recalled. “I had to blow off a lot of steam.”

The next day, Casey felt a weird vibe from the moment he arrived at Nationals Park. There is a certain, unexplainable energy in clubhouses when someone is getting sent down to the minors. In this case, that someone was him. Sean Doolittle, the team’s closer, was going to the injured list. And since the Nationals wanted to add two relievers in his place, they optioned Casey to AAA Rochester.

While Casey packed up his locker in a near-empty clubhouse, Doolittle walked over for a bit of encouragement. Hugging Casey, Doolittle said he would see him soon. He told Casey he’d be back.

“Yeah,” Casey agreed. “I’ll be back.”

***

THE ROAD TO LEHIGH VALLEY, Pennsylvania, foreshadowed the hard road ahead. When the Nationals demoted Casey, he had two options: Wait to travel the next morning to Lehigh Valley, where Rochester was in the middle of a series. Or leave that night with a drive provided by the team.

Casey chose to jet as soon as possible. Again, same as ever, he wanted to get there and get going. About two hours after leaving D.C., the driver asked if they could make a pit stop for caffeine. Casey was cool with it, of course, but after they got back in the car at a roadside gas station, the engine wouldn’t start. Casey made the last leg in an Uber.

Once he was back in Rochester’s lineup, he struggled to find a rhythm. He hit .172 in May with 29 strikeouts. In June, in a road game against the St. Paul Saints, he dove for a flyball and landed awkwardly on his right shoulder. When he went to throw the ball in, he could barely heave it 10 feet. He missed the next two weeks. At that point, he was also still feeling the effects of offseason surgery for a double hernia. When his parents visited Rochester that summer, Casey says they watched him “bawl my eyes out.” Sitting across from them, he would ask the universe what was happening, what he was doing wrong. In late-night voice memos to Mary, he would tell her, through thick tears, that he was not fast enough, not strong enough, not a good enough hitter. But he always finished by saying he wasn’t ready to stop.
IMG_7840 (1) copy.jpg (1679x1243, AR: 1.35)“I was worried it would damage his drive,” Troy, Casey’s father, said. “I think it made him feel like ‘I worked my ass off and it still wasn’t enough.’ And then you have that attitude in your mind, that thought in your head, and I don’t think you perform as well after you’ve been let down. But I was very proud that he just kept working no matter what. Not surprised, but proud.”

One weekend in 2022, during a particularly rough stretch in Casey’s head, Mary drove the seven hours from Boston to Rochester because she felt like he needed her. She bought a ticket in the outfield, right behind where he was playing. And once he noticed her, when she saw the look of relief on his face, she knew she was right.

Baseball is one giant lesson of how to deal with failure. What’s not included, at least not specifically, is how to deal with the pressure of joining a new team in a massive trade, then never getting your chance despite sitting an arm’s length from it for close to a week.

In 2023, the year after his brush with the major leagues, there were times Casey felt a panic attack coming on whenever he got near a batting cage. He worked nonstop with a mental skills coach. When the Nationals asked if he wanted to try pitching in the second half of the season, he was relieved to drop his bat for a while. He wound up throwing one inning in AA, retiring all three batters he faced. But after that season, the Nats released him and he floated into the baseball abyss. No MLB teams called over the winter. In the spring, when Casey was still without a job, his agent raised the idea of playing indie ball in York, Pennsylvania, which had always been an absolute no in Casey’s mind.

But now, well, what the heck. And York wouldn’t just restore his love for baseball, it would lead to a short reunion with the Dodgers, who signed Casey for 30 games with AA Tulsa toward the end of 2024. That was it, though, as far as playing in the states. To make a bit more money, he spent some time in the Mexican League, which was fine, workable, until he spent a Christmas away from Donovan Jr., his firstborn. FaceTime was no longer cutting it. Casey went home.

***

FOR THE LONGEST TIME, ever since Casey and Troy drove from Jersey to Georgia in a red Corvette, hopping from showcase to showcase, hoping the right college coach would show up, home was any place with a batter’s box and outfield grass.

But now it’s Rutland, Vermont, which is near Mary’s family and Donovan’s new job. He works in manufacturing at a GE Aerospace facility. Most mornings, he’s out of the house early for a 7 a.m. shift, leaving before Mary, little Donovan and their newborn son, Callan, are awake. But if there’s overtime to pick up, he usually jumps at it, stretching his shifts from 3 a.m. to 3 p.m., his alarm going off at 2:15.

Once there, he assesses whether individual blades can keep moving down an assembly line that will eventually result in an airplane part. If it’s off by even a thousandth of an inch— or a thou, as they say — it’s a scrap. Casey used to measure his entire life in balls, strikes and the steps to first base. Now the day passes one thou at a time.

“Was I a failure as a human being? No,” Casey said, reflecting on the final years of his baseball career. “But I just felt like I was because I was basing everything off the results of my job. That was my identity for the longest time. I needed something else.”

Dad, it turns out, has been a good alternative. Husband, too. After work, he and Donovan Jr., who’s 3, often play Whiffle ball in the backyard. They each have a popsicle once they’re finished. Some nights, if there’s still time before dinner, they head to the store and buy a matchbox car.
L1023820 copy.jpg (10495x7733, AR: 1.36)It’s not what Casey ever pictured for himself, but that’s only because he never got past baseball, past the next game, past the madcap chase of an almost impossible dream. But it’s nice, he’s finding, being there for dinner, watching his kids grow up in person instead of through a screen. And when Donovan Jr. and Callan go to sleep, he and Mary can sit around and talk, which used to be impossible to schedule between noon and midnight.

If, for some reason, baseball comes up, if they start riffing on what could have been and how to define Donovan Casey, Mary doesn’t budge: Her husband is a big leaguer, once and forever. His dad, his mom, his former coaches, his longtime trainer — they all agree, of course. In April of 2022, someone decided that Casey should be on the Washington Nationals’ roster. They made the necessary calls. Casey got the uniform. His name was on the lineup card, five times over, no matter that it was near the bottom with the other subs.

Casey, though, doesn’t see it that way. When he Googles his name, which he still does sometimes, there’s a blank space where there should be at least one stat — a strikeout or homer or a single game played. He’s never cut corners, doesn’t plan to start now. But the point, he says, is that he doesn’t need the label of big leaguer to be proud of his career. Turns out baseball is a lesson in that, too.

entries.title: Trump Administration Moves to Axe Protection for Undeveloped National Forests
entries.summary: The USDA plans to end the “Roadless Rule,” a prohibition on building roads through about 45 million acres of national forests.
entries.content:
The Trump administration moved Tuesday to end 25 years of restrictions that protected the country’s wildest and largest undisturbed forests from construction and logging.

The Agriculture Department announced that it plans to rescind what’s known as the “Roadless Rule,” which prohibits building new roads through the nation's remaining untouched forests.

President Bill Clinton put the Roadless Rule in place in 2001 after two problems became untenable for the U.S. Forest Service. Most pressing at the time, the agency was failing to maintain the roads that already existed, putting taxpayers on the hook for an increasingly large maintenance backlog bill.

Additionally, new timber and logging projects in untouched areas of national forests were increasingly unpopular with public lands advocates, hunters and conservationists, who warned that many of the country’s iconic ecosystems could fall apart with further development.

The Roadless Rule now protects about 45 million acres of forests, or about one-third of all national forest land managed by the Forest Service.

If the rescission is finalized, it will be easier for the timber industry to push to develop new logging projects in currently untouchable areas that contain millions of acres of valuable, old-growth trees.

USDA said rescinding the Roadless Rule would make it easier for wildland firefighters to build roads to fight fires.

“For too long, outdated restrictions have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities. Today, we filed a proposal to restore authority to local forest managers who know the land best, removing the barriers that have kept them from doing the work the land demands,” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a statement announcing the rescission.

The federal government already grants some exceptions to the Roadless Rule’s prohibition specifically for fire mitigation near areas where people live.

Many firefighting experts argue that a full rescission of the rule for firefighting reasons does not make sense, because the construction of new roads can lead to an increase in human-caused wildfires. Wilderness areas have the lowest number of wildfire ignitions compared to other types of forested areas, a group of wildland fire experts wrote in a letter to Rollins last year.
entries.author: Anna Kramer

entries.title: Rep. Buddy Carter Emerges as a Dark Horse Candidate to Lead the FDA
entries.summary: The Georgia Republican, a licensed pharmacist, lost his Senate primary earlier this year.
entries.content:
The White House is considering Republican Rep. Buddy Carter of Georgia to be the next commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration, a source familiar with the administration’s thinking confirmed Tuesday.

Choosing Carter for the position would be a pivot for the White House. His name has not been on previously reported short lists for the position.

Carter is leaving Congress at the end of the year; a strong Trump ally, he failed to gain the president’s endorsement in his May GOP primary bid for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff’s seat, and he lost the race. He is a licensed pharmacist and previously owned his own pharmacy, Carter’s Pharmacy, for more than three decades. His license is currently active, according to the Georgia Department of Community Health.

“Carter is interested in the position of FDA commissioner and would bring a unique mix of both policy and real world health experience,” the source said in a statement provided to NOTUS. “He’s a bipartisan champion for patients, providers and innovators with strong relationships inside the administration, in the industry and across the aisle.”

The White House has been considering other candidates recommended by the Department of Health and Human Services for more than a month, but has been slow to officially nominate anyone. Its search has left a lane open for a dark horse candidate to enter the running. Domestic Policy Council adviser Heidi Overton and oncologist Jeff Vacirca are also being considered.

Former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary resigned from the position in April as the White House was considering firing him, frustrated over his resistance to approving fruit-flavored cigarettes.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NOTUS.

Carter has also been a consistent defender of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He has said he believes routine childhood vaccines are safe and effective but has backed the secretary’s shifts in federal vaccine guidance and stressed his opposition to government vaccine requirements.

Carter defended the administration’s controversial firing last year of Susan Monarez, the short-lived commissioner of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, saying in a post on X at the time that she took “anti-administration” positions and oversaw an agency that had been “leveraged as a force for liberal ideology.”

President Donald Trump declined to endorse Carter — or any other candidate — in the Republican Senate primary. Carter came in third in the polls, and Rep. Mike Collins (R-Georgia) and former football coach Derek Dooley advanced to a runoff. Trump issued a last-minute endorsement in the runoff for Collins, who went on to win the nomination.

Carter has not endorsed Collins. The Georgia Senate race currently leans Democrat, according to the nonpartisan bellwether Cook Political Report.

Editor's Note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.
entries.author: Paige Winfield Cunningham, Taylor Giorno

entries.title: ABC Lawsuit Accuses the FCC of Running a ‘Retaliatory Campaign’
entries.summary: The company said the FCC has threatened its broadcast licenses in violation of the First Amendment.
entries.content:
ABC filed a lawsuit against the Federal Communications Commission on Tuesday, accusing it of punishing television stations for content President Donald Trump dislikes.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr has threatened ABC’s broadcast licenses and investigated its workplace diversity practices, as well as Democratic Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico’s appearance on “The View.” The complaint contends these moves amount to First Amendment violations.

“The Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts,” the company’s attorneys wrote in the court filing. “That campaign began in this Administration’s earliest days and has only intensified since.”

ABC is seeking emergency intervention from the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to stop the FCC from demanding early renewal for eight of the company’s television stations. None of the licenses was set to expire before 2028, but Carr demanded they file renewals this year. The FCC had not called for early renewals for more than 50 years, according to the complaint.

A spokesperson for the commission said Disney, ABC’s parent company, was engaging in a campaign of disinformation and that the FCC would continue to follow the facts.

The lawsuit highlights Trump’s repeated demands that ABC be stripped of its licenses, including during his July 16 primetime address that ABC didn’t air on broadcast but livestreamed digitally.

“In a rare move, NBC and ABC fake news have both said that they would not cover this speech. They knew what it was about,” Trump said. “They and others in the media are part of a plot. They want to continue this fraud for whatever reason. … You can't have a great country without free and fair elections. Fraud like this should mean a revocation of their licenses.”

Late-night host Jimmy Kimmel’s on-air comments also triggered the FCC’s moves to shape the company’s content, ABC’s lawsuit states. The order to file the license renewals came the day after Trump called for ABC to fire Kimmel for his pre-White House Correspondents Dinner joke referring to first lady Melania Trump as having “a glow like an expectant widow.”

The timing was not related to the president’s comments, Carr said in a Politico interview.

Last year, Carr’s threat to take action against ABC following Kimmel’s remarks on the assasination of Charlie Kirk prompted the company to pull his show for several days.

“We can do this the easy way or the hard way,” Carr said at the time during a podcast interview with right-wing political commentator Benny Johnson. “These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.”

entries.title: ‘Not in Texas’
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for Aug. 18, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Democrats are almost in an “open civil war,” Mike Johnson said while campaigning for Rep. Tom Barrett in Michigan today, calling the representative’s race one of the “top five” America is watching. The House speaker remained confident in Republicans’ ability to buck history and pick up House seats for the sitting president’s party.

  • “I’m sad to say, this is not our father’s Democratic Party,” Johnson said, bashing Democrat William Lawrence. 
Scoop: Rep. Buddy Carter (R-Georgia) has emerged as a candidate for the next FDA commissioner, Paige Winfield Cunningham and Taylor Giorno report. The licensed pharmacist lost his GOP Senate primary in May.





THE ADMINISTRATION

The USDA plans to rescind the “Roadless Rule,” a 25-year-old policy that prohibits building new roads through the nation’s remaining untouched forests.

The DOJ plans to deploy a “historic number” of midterm election monitors. The agency also announced it will conduct election oversight during Florida and Wyoming’s primaries tonight.





THE HILL

Rep. Ralph Norman says Trump has erred in endorsing Sen. Darline Graham to hold South Carolina’s Senate seat. The pair will debate tonight at 7 p.m. before early voting kicks off tomorrow.

  • The GOP representative dropped a new TV ad today saying “the establishment has already picked their candidate. Same old playbook, same old insiders.”
Rep. Seth Moulton's Wikipedia page has gone through a series of revisions today, with users seemingly scrubbing (and unscrubbing) the Democrat's past comments on trans issues ahead of the Massachusetts Senate primary on Sept. 1.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) responded to criticism generated by NOTUS’ scoop that a former staffer went to work for Democrat James Talarico. “Only in authoritarian countries does someone else get to decide where you work,” he posted on X. “Not in Texas.”





THE STATES

Gov. Josh Shapiro signed new restrictions on AI data center development in Pennsylvania today — part of a string of governors (and hopefuls) hoping to build a lane on the issue.

  • Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa released an attack ad against Republican Gov. Greg Abbott on the issue today.




THE COURTS

Minnesota AG Keith Ellison sued Abbott to force the extradition of an ICE agent charged with assault in connection with the government’s immigration operations earlier this year.

  • The agent was arrested in Texas in May but has not faced charges in Minnesota despite repeated attempts from state officials.
ABC filed a suit against the FCC today, accusing the agency of punishing TV stations over content the president dislikes.

A federal judge lifted the last judicial block preventing DHS from ending Ethiopia’s TPS status, affecting more than 5,000 immigrants.
