entries.title: Six D.C. Police Employees Accused of Taking $440,000 in Fraudulent OT
entries.summary: A judge signed arrest warrants for the six current and former employees on Tuesday.
entries.content:
A judge signed arrest warrants for six current and former D.C. police employees Tuesday after authorities accused them of collecting nearly half a million dollars combined for overtime they did not work.

The employees — a former sergeant, two officers, one former senior police officer, a former lieutenant and a civilian employee — will be charged with fraud, theft and forgery, according to news releases from the D.C. attorney general’s office and the U.S. attorney's office for D.C. They will also be charged with uttering, which means presenting a document one knows is fake or forged.

The arrests come as D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department is struggling to curb soaring overtime costs and grappling with a 50-year staffing low. For many officers, overtime has become an increasingly common and exhausting necessity in recent years, as higher-ups have frequently canceled officers’ days off to staff the department’s vast list of responsibilities — including 911 calls, protests and security for international conferences and traveling dignitaries.

But for this group of six, prosecutors allege, overtime became a lucrative, illegal scheme.

Internal investigators with the D.C. police department began looking into the alleged scheme when they saw irregularities in overtime submissions in the Fifth District, where the accused officers were working at the time, according to prosecutors. The investigators ultimately found that a group of employees in the district’s administrative office had routinely submitted false information about hours worked, including hours when they were not working or were otherwise unavailable. In some cases, they claimed overtime while traveling, both domestically and abroad, prosecutors said.

Former Sgt. Frantz Fulcher fraudulently received nearly $175,000, prosecutors allege. Officer Dorrie Smith-Cleere allegedly received more than $87,000, and Officer Thomas Krmenec allegedly received more than $89,000. Former Senior Officer Bernadette Richardson improperly collected more than $43,000. Former Lt. Peter Sheldon and civilian employee Johnnie Dyer were improperly paid $18,000 and $27,000, respectively, according to prosecutors.

The police employees could not immediately be reached for comment.

“These six officers abused their positions of power, exploiting the District and the residents they took an oath to serve and protect. No one is above the law, especially those trusted with enforcing it,” D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb said in a statement. The chief of Schwalb’s public corruption section has been detailed to the U.S. attorney’s office to serve as lead prosecutor on the case.

The allegedly fraudulent payments represent a small fraction of the department’s overtime spending. Last fiscal year, the department spent nearly $134 million on overtime — a whopping sum that police officials have said they hope to reduce by filling staffing gaps.

The earnings of most of the accused officers were also small compared to some of the highest-paid D.C. police employees, who take overtime to extremes. Last fiscal year, the department’s top 25 earners made between $200,000 and $374,000 each in overtime alone, often doubling or tripling their salaries, according to documents D.C. police submitted to the D.C. Council. These top earners routinely log 14- to 18-hour work days, back to back, previous reporting has found.
entries.author: Jenny Gathright

entries.title: Preservation Group Urges the Supreme Court to Stop Trump's Ballroom
entries.summary: The project would be almost impossible to take down once it’s completed, the National Trust for Historic Preservation says.
entries.content:
The National Trust for Historic Preservation asked the Supreme Court on Tuesday to block the Trump administration’s ballroom construction while a legal challenge to the project plays out in court.

The filing is in response to an application from the Trump administration last week that asked the court to lift a lower-court ruling that would halt work Friday.

“Each court to examine the question has agreed that [the administration has] no unilateral legal authority — constitutional, statutory, or otherwise — to build a massive ballroom on the site of the now-demolished East Wing,” the filing says. “And each court has told [the administration] in no uncertain terms that they must stop their illegal construction unless and until they receive express approval from Congress.”

The National Trust argued that it and the public will suffer irreparable harm if the court lifts the injunction. It pointed to the administration’s assertion that the project would be almost impossible to take down once it’s completed, and said that is part of the administration’s strategy.

“Petitioners make no secret of the fact that if the Court permits construction to continue, they will declare the case over,” the filing says.

The group also told the justices that the Trump administration would not be harmed if construction remained paused, since the project isn’t close to being finished. The administration previously estimated that construction would continue for roughly two more years.

The National Trust offered an expedited legal process to offset the administration’s concerns about a delay that would include Supreme Court oral arguments over the ballroom construction as soon as October.

The filing says that a few weeks of delay for “a project that will not be complete for years is far outweighed by the irreparable harm of the completion of a structure at the White House that Petitioners themselves assert will be ‘virtually impossible to deconstruct.’”

Should the court uphold the injunction, work could still continue on the underground military facility. A federal appeals court in D.C. stopped construction of the ballroom, but not the military complex that would exist beneath it.

That court ruled the ballroom couldn’t be built without congressional approval, which the administration has tried and failed to obtain.

In its application to the Supreme Court last week, the administration argued that the ballroom project — described in the filing as an “integrated military complex” that is “required for national security” — was necessary for the safety of the president, his family and administration staff.

Although the project’s initial description included a secure ballroom for events on the White House grounds, its scope has broadened into a drone hub with military infrastructure and facilities for the Secret Service.

President Donald Trump has continued to say that the entire project will be built by private donations. However, The Washington Post has reported that documents from a contractor said tax money will pay for roughly half of the $600 million ballroom project.
entries.author: Ben T.N. Mause

entries.title: DOJ Plans to Deploy a ‘Historic Number’ of Midterm Election Monitors
entries.summary: The department also announced Tuesday it was monitoring primaries in Florida and Wyoming.
entries.content:
The Department of Justice is mobilizing a veritable army of election monitors in swing states across the country for this year’s midterm elections, Harmeet K. Dhillon, head of the department’s Civil Rights Division, revealed in an interview this week.

At least 1,000 Trump administration-trained and -approved workers will oversee voting in a number of precincts, a total that is “probably going to be a historic number for a Republican administration,” Dhillon told Bloomberg on Monday.

The announcement comes after months of President Donald Trump repeating debunked claims of widespread voter fraud, a message that he has made central to his second term.

On Tuesday, the DOJ also announced that it would be conducting election oversight during primaries in Florida and Wyoming, both states with contentious House and Senate elections that could tip the balance of power in Congress.

Dhillon is a Trump ally who has been working on election monitoring for months. She was nominated by Trump in December 2024 and confirmed by the Senate in April 2025.

In a press release, the department noted that it has deployed over 75 monitors across five states — including the Michigan and Arizona primaries — at over 200 polling locations this primary season.

“Election monitoring is an ongoing priority for this office,” Dhillon said in a press release. “Nondiscriminatory monitoring ensures all elections remain free, fair, and accessible to all.”

In Tuesday’s primaries, the department will have approximately four Civil Rights Division attorneys monitoring polls in Miami-Dade County, Florida, and two Civil Rights Division attorneys in Laramie County, Wyoming.

In an interview with Bloomberg published Monday, Dhillon said the monitors being sent to polling sites are there to observe whether elections are being conducted fairly.

Dhillon said the department’s actions are in tune with the administration’s policies and measures taken in previous elections. The training for potential election watchers would be the same used by past administrations, she added.

“We just did it in the primary. We will do it to the tune of approximately 1,000 election monitors in the November election,” she told Bloomberg. “This is something that DOJ does.”

Under former President Joe Biden, the department launched similar efforts, sending poll monitors to 22 states during the 2022 midterm elections and 27 states during the 2024 presidential election.

Dhillon has also mounted an ill-fated effort to obtain sensitive voting records from states — including nonpublic information such as partial Social Security numbers. She described it as an effort to make sure people are properly registered to vote, but the department has lost 23 out of the 31 federal lawsuits it filed against states and Washington, D.C., to force jurisdictions to hand over the unredacted voter registration data.

The effort remains ongoing.

Denied a high-profile courtroom victory, Trump has instead taken to pushing an elections bill called the SAVE America Act, describing it repeatedly as his highest priority. The act has passed the House but is stalled in the Senate, where Majority Leader John Thune has said the bill is effectively dead.

The measure would mandate that people provide proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections and require states to implement photo ID checks at polling places. Democrats have harshly criticized the act, saying it would disenfranchise millions of Americans.

Trump has also refused to rule out declaring an election-security-related state of emergency before the midterms, though Dhillon said she has not been a part of those discussions.
entries.author: Torrie Herrington

entries.title: White House’s University Antisemitism Probes Had ‘Predetermined’ Outcomes, Whistleblowers Say
entries.summary: A group of DOJ civil rights attorneys say the investigations into Harvard, Brown and Columbia were “subordinate to political priorities.”
entries.content:
The Trump administration’s antisemitism investigations into Ivy League universities were rushed and had “predetermined” outcomes meant to force the institutions into paying out settlements, a former Justice Department lawyer alleges in a new whistleblower complaint.

The claims were brought forth by Haley Van Erem, a former DOJ attorney assigned to work on the investigations through the Department of Health and Human Services, and other career civil rights attorneys whose names were redacted in the public version of the complaint, released by House Judiciary Democrats. The group describes an “outcome‑driven approach” taken by a multiagency task force that was “subordinate to political priorities,” alleging that those who brought forward disagreements were sidelined or faced reprimands.

The White House created a sweeping task force last year to “root out antisemitic harassment” in response to pro-Palestinian student groups protesting Israel’s actions in Gaza following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks. Under President Donald Trump’s administration, officials investigated dozens of the country’s top schools — including Harvard University, Brown University and Columbia University, which are at the center of Tuesday’s whistleblower report — and canceled hundreds of millions in grant money by claiming the institutions were violating Jewish and Israeli students’ Title VI rights. Those fights over federal dollars eventually led to settlements and ongoing litigation.

When attorneys assigned to the investigations detailed a lack of evidence of civil rights violations or settlements that preempted finished work, senior DOJ and HHS officials dismissed those concerns, says the complaint, which was sent to multiple congressional committees.

“[Ms. Van Erem and her colleagues] believe based on HHS officials’ actions that the outcomes of the investigations were predetermined, without regard to the evidence,” the report states. “Hundreds of millions of dollars were suspended from these universities prior to the completion of Title VI investigations and the investigative team’s conclusions were frequently disregarded.”

The investigators were pushed to complete their investigations in 45 days, despite their objections to that timeline, the report says. At Brown University, investigators did not find any violations of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act — which prohibits discrimination based on race or national origin for programs that receive federal funding — but an HHS official said higher-ups would never accept that result, the complaint says.

Daniel Shieh, the associate deputy director at the HHS’ civil rights office, had “acknowledged that the team had done a good job convincing the front office that they should move on from Brown, but unspecified ‘stakeholders’ had ‘approached the Task Force’ demanding action,” the complaint says. “Ms. Van Erem left federal service shortly after this meeting.”

A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement that Van Erem did not work on university investigations during her time at the department. Van Erem stopped working for the federal government on May 30, 2025, according to the report.

“And for all matters, the Department stands behind the integrity of these investigations,” the spokesperson said.

HHS, Columbia and Harvard did not respond to a request for comment.

The whistleblowers’ allegations follow recent criticism from federal judges who say government lawyers have increasingly presented misleading evidence in court and assert that Trump’s DOJ is flouting a longtime presumption of good-faith cases.

The agencies also assigned investigators to interview Middle East studies faculty who weren’t connected to complaints of antisemitism, the report says, and were given just a few hours to examine documents that would justify suspending hundreds of millions of dollars worth of grants from Columbia.

Both Columbia and Brown reached deals with the Trump administration, with Columbia agreeing to pay more than $220 million to restore its research funding. Brown entered into an agreement to give $50 million to workforce development organizations in its home state of Rhode Island.

“We made clear when announcing Brown's resolution with the government that the agreement was not a result of any determination of fault by any government agency, and Brown denied any fault or violation of federal law,” Brian Clark, vice president for news and strategic campus communications, told NOTUS in a statement. “In contrast with other universities, Brown had not been informed of a reason for the freeze of its federal research funding, and at no time was Brown informed of any finding that the University violated any law.”

The investigation into Harvard was not completed before the university sued the Trump administration in a matter that remains ongoing in a federal appeals court. In December, a federal judge ruled the administration had unlawfully frozen in $2 billion research funds.
entries.author: Jackie Llanos

entries.title: Debbie Wasserman Schultz Wins Primary in Historically Black District
entries.summary: Wasserman Schultz, who is white, prevailed after Democratic critics accused her of undermining Black representation.
entries.content:
Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz was projected to win a competitive Democratic primary in a historically Black district in Florida, likely securing her return to the House of Representatives in January.

The Associated Press called the race for Wasserman Schultz on Tuesday night.

Wasserman Schultz had been under heavy scrutiny from Democratic officials for choosing to run in Florida’s 20th Congressional District, which has long been represented by a Black lawmaker and has a plurality Black population. Wasserman Schultz, the only white candidate in the race, ran against four Black Democrats after redistricting effectively eliminated her current seat.

Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis signed legislation that redrew Florida’s congressional maps in an effort to bolster his party’s chances of picking up seats in the 2026 midterms.

Wasserman Schultz, best known for her role as chair of the Democratic National Committee during the 2016 election cycle, lives in the new 22nd Congressional District, which now leans Republican. She hopped in the race for Florida’s 20th Congressional District, one of the safest blue seats in the state, in late May. The lawmaker will face Brent Andersen, who won the Republican nomination Tuesday.

The lawmaker’s decision to run in a district that Black lawmakers have represented for more than three decades comes amid concerns from the Congressional Black Caucus that many of its members will not be returning after the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965, allowing states to eliminate race-based districts.

Wasserman Schultz faced backlash from Black Democrats from the launch of her campaign: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries declined to endorse her in the race multiple times; CBC Chair Yvette Clark told Politico that her decision to run in a district that has been historically represented by a Black person was “painful,” after Wasserman Schultz suggested that the CBC encouraged her to run; and a number of Black officials in the state have denounced her.

Despite the intraparty anger aimed at Wasserman Schultz, she benefited from the crowded primary, which ultimately divided the primary vote against her. The lawmaker ran against embattled former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, who held the seat until she resigned in April but once again ran for reelection, former Broward County Mayor Dale Holness, activist Elijah Manley and rapper Luther “Uncle Luke” Campbell.

Shortly after the AP called the race, Manley told NOTUS over text that he called Wasserman Schultz to concede the race.

“She said thank you, and that it was the first time someone in the same race as her has ever called to concede,” Manley said.

This story has been updated with the race call for the Republican nomination in the district and a comment from Elijah Manley.
entries.author: Oriana González

entries.title: The Democrats Turning to Republicans For Votes
entries.summary: In a polarized political environment Democrats are trying to show they can work across the aisle with endorsements from Republicans.
entries.content:
With key races in red and purple states like Texas, Alaska, Georgia and Arizona, Democrats are turning to Republican validators to help them win statewide contests.

Candidates are trotting out endorsements from prominent Republican officials, and even bringing some on to join their campaigns. Many of these contests are in states where the GOP has a significant registration advantage, or recent statewide contests have been extremely close, so nabbing some share of the vote from those who haven’t pulled the lever for a Democrat before is essential.

“Every Democrat says we need a bigger tent, but it’s up to each candidate to show that they actually mean it,” said Andrew Mamo, a spokesperson for The Bench, a group that has boosted center-left Democrats in contested races this cycle.

Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico poached a staffer from Republican Sen. John Cornyn’s Senate office to serve as deputy policy director, an unheard of move in today’s partisan environment that has drawn criticism from some on the left and on the right.

“My message to Texans across the political spectrum is clear: no matter which party you belong to, which part of the state you’re from, or which candidate you supported in the primary — you have a place in this campaign,” Talarico said in a statement explaining the hire.

Talarico is running against Texas state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who defeated Cornyn in the Republican primary runoff earlier this year. Paxton’s scandals have troubled some Republicans in the state, giving Democrats hope that this year could finally be their chance to flip a seat that hasn’t been represented by a Democrat in over 30 years.

Cornyn on Tuesday urged conservatives criticizing him over his staffer’s decision to join Talarico’s campaign to work harder at strengthening their party’s appeal.

“Those concerned might want to channel their energy into broadening R[epublican] outreach to a coalition of voters rather than just those already converted,” Cornyn wrote in a post online on Tuesday.

Democratic candidates, Mamo said, need “show not tell moments that say, ‘Hello GOP & Indy voters, I’m not your average Democrat and I’m ok making some people mad in order to win your support.’ That’s how we go from talking about a big tent to building it.”

Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff announced endorsements by three Republicans, including former Arizona Sen. Jeff Flake and two local Georgia mayors, earlier this month, in his reelection bid for a second term against Rep. Mike Collins, the Republican nominee in the race.

Flake, who also endorsed Democratic President Joe Biden in 2020, cited Ossoff’s character, constituent work, and commitment to the institution of the Senate as reasons why he chose to back the freshman Democrat, who’s been getting a lot of 2028 presidential buzz lately.

“Endorsements overall are overrated,” Flake said in an interview with NOTUS. “But cross-party endorsements can help and have helped in the past. I think it's a smart strategy."

Another Arizona politician, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs, is making a similar play for independent and GOP voters. Hobbs recently selected John Giles, a Republican former Mesa mayor, as her running mate for lieutenant governor this year. Giles also endorsed Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

“The one thing you hear in swing voter focus groups over and over again is exhaustion with politics,” said Democratic political strategist Steve Schale, who’s not involved in the Arizona race. “Her math problem is similar to [Talarico], and the thing is, it really doesn't lose her much … Even in Democratic primaries, the trait ‘can work with Republicans to get things done’ usually polls pretty strong.”

“Hobbs is making a bet — that appears to be working — that voters are just over it and want grown ass adults to get things done. I love it — and I wish more Dems in lean Red states running for Governor would do it,” he said.

And in Alaska, a Senate battleground in 2026, Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola is hoping that voters will view her rejection of financial support from Harris — who is viewed negatively by most Republicans in the state — as evidence of her independent streak. President Donald Trump won Alaska by 13 points in 2024, and an association with national Democrats would likely hurt Peltola’s campaign in the red state.

Democrats have tried this strategy before, including in the last three presidential elections, to varying success. Biden narrowly beat Trump in 2020 in purple states by similarly touting Republican endorsements. In 2024, Harris even teamed up with former Rep. Liz Cheney (R-Wyoming), campaigning with her to make appeals to Republicans who were uneasy about Donald Trump. She went on to lose anyway.

National Republicans believe it also won’t work this year.

“Democrats trying to appeal to Republican voters is like a career criminal suddenly running for sheriff,” said Natalie Baldassarre, the national press secretary for the Republican National Committee. “All of these far-left extremists support open borders, higher taxes and endless government control. Democrats should get their own house in order before they come looking for new voters.”
entries.author: Igor Bobic

entries.title: Court Declines to Overturn EPA Designation of Two ‘Forever Chemicals’
entries.summary: The “hazardous substance” designation expands federal power to hold parties accountable for cleaning up releases.
entries.content:
A federal court on Tuesday upheld the Environmental Protection Agency’s designation of two “forever chemicals,” PFOA and PFOS, as hazardous substances.

The designation expands the federal government’s power to hold parties that release chemicals into the environment liable for their cleanup under the Superfund law, also known as CERCLA. It also creates requirements for notifications when more than one pound of those chemicals are released.

PFOA and PFOS are part of a larger group known as PFAS chemicals, which are linked to certain kinds of cancer and other negative health outcomes. PFAS are widespread in the environment and in drinking water, and are present in the blood of almost every person in the United States.

“This decision is a major win for contaminated communities across the country,” Jonathan Kalmuss-Katz, an attorney with Earthjustice, said in a statement. “For too long, industrial polluters have profited from the release of toxic PFAS while sticking taxpayers and communities with the bill when those releases need to be cleaned up.”

The chemicals don’t break down easily in the environment and they accumulate in human bodies — two properties the EPA cited when designated PFOA and PFOS as hazardous substances in 2024. But the ubiquity of the chemicals also creates a complex landscape for legal accountability.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and several industry groups, including the American Chemistry Council and the National Waste and Recycling Association, argued the EPA didn’t do enough to consider the costs that businesses and local organizations may have to bear and didn’t do enough to prove that “substantial danger” was certain to occur when PFOA or PFOS were released into the environment.

Judges at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit shot down those arguments. “To require absolute scientific certainty as to what will happen upon every individual release of a dangerous chemical would have been to legislatively paralyze CERCLA,” Judge Patricia Millett wrote in Tuesday’s opinion.

The EPA’s designation of PFOA and PFOS as hazardous substances created anxiety for chemical companies and so-called “passive receivers” like landfills and wastewater treatment plants, who worried they could be on the hook for cleaning up a widespread chemical.

The EPA has said it will not pursue municipal waste sites, farmers or local fire departments or airports for enforcement.

But Daryl Joseffer, president of the litigation center at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, said in an email after the decision that the EPA failed to consider the costs and consequences of the “hazardous substance” designation, which he argued would cause local governments and businesses to put resources into legal battles.

“EPA’s failure to consider costs and consequences, as required by law, produced a deeply flawed rule that is more likely to spawn unnecessary, costly litigation than to drive expeditious, effective cleanup focused on actual risk,” Joseffer said.

Industry groups that sued the EPA said companies have already seen increased expenses related to the designation.

But for communities that have been pushing for industries to clean up PFAS contamination, that’s a welcome change.

Emily Donovan, a co-founder of Clean Cape Fear, an advocacy group pushing for the cleanup of a Chemours site in North Carolina, called the decision a “common-sense and moral victory.”

“The land belongs to the people and PFAS polluters must pay when they poison sacred resources like our water, air, soil and food supplies. The court agreed unanimously,” Donovan said.
entries.author: Mara Hoplamazian

entries.title: Texas Won’t Send an ICE Agent to Minnesota to Face Charges for a Shooting
entries.summary: In a race against the clock, Minnesota sued to force extradition of the agent on charges of assault with a deadly weapon.
entries.content:
Minnesota sued Texas Gov. Greg Abbott on Tuesday in an attempt to force the state of Texas to hand over an arrested ICE agent accused of committing a crime on the job during Operation Metro Surge when he was stationed up north earlier this year.

Minnesota is in a race against the clock. State officials say there are only nine more days to extradite the agent before a mandatory release kicks in under Texas law, and they fear he will be released and flee to avoid prosecution.

The interstate tensions at play threaten to create the first major showdown between blue and red states over the conduct of agents working for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which has been deployed in Democratic-leaning cities as part of the White House’s nationwide aggressive immigration-enforcement push.

A Hennepin County District Court judge issued a nationwide warrant for the federal agent, Christian Jeremiah Castro, after finding probable cause that the agent in January fired a gun at the front door of a Minneapolis home when he knew there were several people inside and that one of the bullets struck a Venezuelan man, Julio Sosa-Celis.

Four months after the shooting, Hennepin County prosecutors criminally charged Castro with four separate counts of assault with a deadly weapon and falsely reporting a crime. According to the complaint, Castro told the FBI he’d been hit by a broom and a snow shovel while he was chasing someone on the home’s front lawn just before the shooting, but video evidence showed that “Victim 1 tossed the shovel onto the ground, where it remained throughout the incident, and stepped back toward the front door of the home.”

The Hennepin County Attorney’s Office said “the bullet traveled through the door and struck Mr. Sosa-Celis’s leg, before making its final impact in the wall of a child’s room.”

Investigators with the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension traveled south to witness local Texas Rangers arrest Castro on May 29, and he’s been held at the Cameron County Jail.

However, he’s been in custody now for 81 days — and time is running out for Texas to conduct the kind of routine interstate transfer of prisoners that happens hundreds of times a day across the country.

On Tuesday, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a federal lawsuit in Texas asking a federal judge to declare that Abbott’s “withholding of a governor’s rendition warrant for Christian Castro is unconstitutional and unlawful.”

“He has no discretion, I repeat, he has no discretion to decline to do so. None. Yet Castro is still not here to face justice,” Ellison said at a press conference Tuesday morning.

Minnesota law-enforcement officials say that Abbott has simply ignored repeated requests for assistance. Ellison said Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty’s July 30 letter to the Texas governor went unanswered, as did his own Aug. 13 letter warning Abbott that Texas had until 5 p.m. Monday to send Castro north — or face a lawsuit.

A spokesperson with Abbott’s office said Tuesday afternoon that the governor would not be commenting on “pending extradition matters.”

In its lawsuit, Minnesota asks that a federal judge block Texas from simply running out the clock and releasing Castro, citing what it called “a substantial risk that Castro will flee and avoid prosecution in Minnesota.”

ICE does not appear to be publicly standing in the way, as the agency has distanced itself from the agent in question. The Department of Homeland Security told NOTUS on Tuesday that Castro is one of two officers who have been placed on administrative leave pending an internal investigation. DHS said officials at ICE and the Justice Department have reviewed “video evidence” that contradicts what these agents initially reported.

“Lying under oath is a serious federal offense. The U.S. Attorney’s Office is actively investigating these false statements,” DHS said by email through a spokesperson who did not identify themselves.

In Texas, the Minnesota officials are being represented locally by Austin lawyer George Chapman Lobb, whose firm website calls Abbott, the state’s two senators and its attorney general “a bunch of criminal fascists who are enabled by that unstable demented derelict living in the White House.”
entries.author: Jose Pagliery
